From about 1998 to 2008 I collected discarded PCs and parts to build used systems for myself, friends, and donations. Very little of that time was spent weeding out broken parts and polishing up the working ones. By far most of the time I invested was researching motherboards, BIOSes and video cards to find different combinations which would work together in Windows. Why?

  • Matching the connectors between the parts and the motherboard may ensure electrical connectivity, but that doesn't mean those parts will work together. CPU, memory, and video cards all require specific motherboard logic and minimal BIOS features to even power up the machine. Even then, poorly written firmware can prevent certain devices from working together.
  • Then you have to worry about whether Windows can automatically allocate motherboard resources for all the devices without making a mess. You'll know Windows made a mess if the drivers refuse to install or if the system refuses to boot or freezes after a few minutes.
  • After that, you have to worry about whether drivers exist for the Windows version you're using.
  • Then you have to worry that the outdated drivers for the device from that defunct manufacturer you downloaded from a third party archive may have malware bundled with it.
  • Then you have to worry that the drivers don't step on each others' toes. Your sound card make work fine until you install drivers for your ethernet card. After that, you're digging up a new pair of cards.
  • Windows installation takes at least two hours and requires several reboots. Every driver installation requires more reboots.
  • Windows update ... forget using your computer for two days.

Nowadays I just download a Linux ISO and boot from it. The install process takes less than 20 minutes, and I'm ready to play after the first boot. There is almost never a need to install drivers. If any drivers are needed, they are available from either the distro or the manufacturer. Most things are ready to work without any effort on my part. Updates are waiting, and the first update cycle will take 5 minutes. Reboots can be safely delayed until it's convenient for me.

I have to say though, Macs are even easier than Linux. Apple makes the computer and the software, so it all works together out of the box. Updates are a thing, but similar to Linux they are few and safely delayed.

TLDR: I wasted about 10 years building a skill set that is now completely useless outside the rarest circumstances. FML.
